method: The authors synthesized layered transition-metal oxyhalides and performed angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) to map the electronic band structure.
result: They observed intrinsic flat bands that remain stable at room temperature, with orbital selectivity and tunability via material composition.
conclusion: These materials provide a tunable platform for studying strongly correlated electron states at room temperature, potentially enabling new quantum phenomena.

title: Probing Quantum Anomalous Hall States In Twisted Bilayer ${\mathrm{WSe}}_{2}$ Via Attractive Polaron Spectroscopy
authors: Beini Gao, Mahdi Ghafariasl, Mahmoud Jalali Mehrabad, Tsung-Sheng Huang, Lifu Zhang, Deric Session, Pranshoo Upadhyay, Rundong Ma, Ghadah Alshalan, Daniel Suarez, Supratik Sarkar, Suji Park, Houk Jang, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Ming Xie, You Zhou, And Mohammad Hafezi
abstract:
Author(s): Beini Gao, Mahdi Ghafariasl, Mahmoud Jalali Mehrabad, Tsung-Sheng Huang, Lifu Zhang, Deric Session, Pranshoo Upadhyay, Rundong Ma, Ghadah Alshalan, Daniel Suarez, Supratik Sarkar, Suji Park, Houk Jang, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Ming Xie, You Zhou, and Mohammad Hafezi

Magneto-optical spectroscopy of twisted WSe
[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021037] Published Mon May 18, 2026.
tldr: This paper reports magneto-optical spectroscopy of twisted bilayer WSe2, revealing a quantum anomalous Hall phase and electric-field control of magnetic order.
motivation: To probe and control quantum anomalous Hall states in twisted bilayer WSe2, a moiré material with potential for topological phases.
method: Magneto-optical spectroscopy, specifically attractive polaron spectroscopy, is used to study the electronic and magnetic properties under electric and magnetic fields.
result: Observation of a spontaneous quantum anomalous Hall phase and demonstration of electric-field-driven transitions between ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic orders.
conclusion: Twisted bilayer WSe2 hosts tunable quantum anomalous Hall states, offering a platform for exploring topological phases and magnetic order.

title: Could Living Cells Use Phase Transitions To Process Information?
authors: Arvind Murugan, David Zwicker, Charlotta Lorenz, And Eric R. Dufresne
abstract:
Author(s): Arvind Murugan, David Zwicker, Charlotta Lorenz, and Eric R. Dufresne

This Perspective explores biomolecular condensation as a powerful framework for computation, enabling cells to process high-dimensional information to sense, classify, and respond to complex environmental signals.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 020501] Published Tue May 12, 2026.
tldr: This perspective explores how biomolecular condensation in living cells can process high-dimensional information through phase transitions.
motivation: Cells must process complex environmental signals, and biomolecular condensates may offer a powerful computational framework.
method: The authors discuss theoretical concepts of phase separation and condensation as information-processing mechanisms.
result: They propose that phase transitions enable cells to sense, classify, and respond to high-dimensional inputs.
conclusion: Biomolecular condensation is a promising paradigm for cellular computation, but the connection to quantum information or thermodynamics is not established.

title: Liquid-Gas Criticality Of Hyperuniform Fluids
authors: Shang Gao, Hao Shang, Hao Hu, Yu-Qiang Ma, And Qun-Li Lei
abstract:
Author(s): Shang Gao, Hao Shang, Hao Hu, Yu-Qiang Ma, and Qun-Li Lei

Where ordinary fluids show wild fluctuations and critical opalescence, hyperuniform fluids of spinning particles stay unusually calm yet highly susceptible at the liquid–vapor critical point.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021032] Published Mon May 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the liquid-gas criticality of hyperuniform fluids, a topic in soft condensed matter physics.
motivation: To understand the critical behavior of hyperuniform fluids, which exhibit suppressed density fluctuations at large scales.
method: The authors use theoretical analysis and simulations to investigate the liquid-vapor critical point of hyperuniform fluids composed of spinning particles.
result: Hyperuniform fluids show unusual calmness yet high susceptibility at the critical point, contrasting with ordinary fluids.
conclusion: The findings reveal unique critical phenomena in hyperuniform fluids, relevant to statistical mechanics but not to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Stealthy-Hyperuniform Wave Dynamics In Two-Dimensional Photonic Crystals
authors: Maria Barsukova, Zeyu Zhang, Brian Gould, Koorosh Sadri, Christian Rosiek, Søren Stobbe, Jonas Karcher, And Mikael C. Rechtsman
abstract:
Author(s): Maria Barsukova, Zeyu Zhang, Brian Gould, Koorosh Sadri, Christian Rosiek, Søren Stobbe, Jonas Karcher, and Mikael C. Rechtsman

While disordered stealthy hyperuniform materials are expected to be largely transparent within a particular range of wavelengths, new experiments on large-scale silicon photonic crystals reveal unexpected residual scattering driven by radiative loss.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021028] Published Thu May 07, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies wave dynamics in stealthy hyperuniform photonic crystals, revealing unexpected residual scattering due to radiative loss.
motivation: Stealthy hyperuniform materials are expected to be transparent in certain wavelength ranges, but experiments show unexpected scattering that needs explanation.
method: Large-scale experiments on silicon photonic crystals combined with theoretical analysis to characterize the scattering behavior.
result: Residual scattering is driven by radiative loss, contradicting the expectation of transparency.
conclusion: The findings highlight limitations of stealthy hyperuniformity for photonic applications and provide insights into wave dynamics in disordered systems.

title: Ballistic Spin Valve In Graphene Realized Via Electron Optics
authors: Daniel Burrow, Oktay Deveci, Rares Dragomir, Thomas Thomson, And Ivan J. Vera-Marun
abstract:
Author(s): Daniel Burrow, Oktay Deveci, Rares Dragomir, Thomas Thomson, and Ivan J. Vera-Marun

Transverse magnetic focusing in encapsulated graphene reveals gate-tunable ballistic spin transport, providing a mechanism for coherent spin control through spin-dependent electron optics.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021029] Published Thu May 07, 2026.
tldr: This paper demonstrates a ballistic spin valve in graphene using transverse magnetic focusing and electron optics.
motivation: To achieve coherent spin control and realize a spin valve in graphene via ballistic transport and electron optics.
method: Transverse magnetic focusing in encapsulated graphene is used to reveal gate-tunable ballistic spin transport.
result: Observation of ballistic spin transport and coherent spin control through spin-dependent electron optics.
conclusion: The work provides a mechanism for spin control in graphene using electron optics, relevant for spintronics.

title: Dipolar Nematic State In Relaxor Ferroelectrics
authors: Yuan-Jinsheng Liu, Tyler C. Sterling, And Shi Liu
abstract:
Author(s): Yuan-Jinsheng Liu, Tyler C. Sterling, and Shi Liu

A nematic ordering underpins the behavior of relaxor ferroelectrics.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021022] Published Wed Apr 29, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies the dipolar nematic state in relaxor ferroelectrics, a condensed matter physics topic.
motivation: Relaxor ferroelectrics exhibit complex ordering; understanding the nematic state is key to their behavior.
method: The authors likely use experimental or theoretical methods to characterize the dipolar nematic phase.
result: They identify a dipolar nematic ordering that underpins relaxor ferroelectric properties.
conclusion: The work advances understanding of relaxor ferroelectrics but has no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Provable Quantum Speedups For Computing Persistence In Topological Data Analysis
authors: Casper Gyurik, Alexander Schmidhuber, Robbie King, Vedran Dunjko, And Ryu Hayakawa
abstract:
Author(s): Casper Gyurik, Alexander Schmidhuber, Robbie King, Vedran Dunjko, and Ryu Hayakawa

A quantum algorithm achieving exponential speedup for a topological data analysis problem is proposed, potentially driving new practical applications in quantum computing.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020361] Published Tue Jun 16, 2026.
tldr: A quantum algorithm for computing persistence in topological data analysis is proposed, claiming exponential speedup.
motivation: Topological data analysis is a powerful tool for analyzing high-dimensional data, but classical algorithms for computing persistence are computationally expensive. Quantum computing may offer speedups.
method: The paper presents a quantum algorithm that leverages quantum linear algebra and topological data analysis techniques to compute persistence diagrams.
result: The algorithm achieves a provable exponential speedup over classical methods for certain instances.
conclusion: This work demonstrates a potential quantum advantage in topological data analysis, but the practical relevance to quantum information theory or quantum thermodynamics is limited.

title: Grand Challenge Of Quantum Applications
authors: Ryan Babbush, Robbie King, Sergio Boixo, William Huggins, Tanuj Khattar, Guang Hao Low, Jarrod R. Mcclean, Thomas O’brien, And Nicholas C. Rubin
abstract:
Author(s): Ryan Babbush, Robbie King, Sergio Boixo, William Huggins, Tanuj Khattar, Guang Hao Low, Jarrod R. McClean, Thomas O’Brien, and Nicholas C. Rubin

A proposed five-stage framework outlines the path to useful quantum computing, detailing the scientific milestones required to bridge the gap between theory and real-world utility.


[PRX Quantum 7, 020101] Published Mon Jun 15, 2026.
tldr: This paper proposes a five-stage framework for achieving useful quantum computing, outlining scientific milestones.
motivation: To bridge the gap between theoretical quantum computing and real-world utility by providing a structured roadmap.
method: The authors propose a five-stage framework based on their expertise and analysis of current quantum computing progress.
result: A high-level roadmap with stages from quantum advantage to fault-tolerant quantum computing, but no specific technical results.
conclusion: The framework serves as a guide for the quantum computing community to focus efforts on key milestones.

title: 2d Van Der Waals Magnets: From Fundamental Physics To Applications
authors: Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, And Nuh Gedik
abstract:
Author(s): Je-Geun Park, Kai-Xuan Zhang, Hyeonsik Cheong, Jae Hoon Kim, Carina A. Belvin, David Hsieh, Honglie Ning, and Nuh Gedik

Scientific discovery is often described as walking into a dark room and turning on the light. The discovery of 2D magnetism in van der Waals materials in 2016 was one such leap forward, removing one spatial dimension from macroscopic materials. The study of 2D magnets has challenged established theories and uncovered new phenomena. This review summarizes the current state of knowledge of magnetic phenomena in 2D van der Waals materials. The field encompasses not just the traditional study of ferromagnets and antiferromagnets but also topology, quantum and nonequilibrium dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons and spintronics, and the interaction of magnetism with light, phonons, and electric fields (multiferroics). The field is actively evolving, expanding theoretical understanding, materials capabilities, and experimental phenomenology while opening new directions for application.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025003] Published Wed May 27, 2026.
tldr: A review of 2D van der Waals magnets covering fundamental physics and applications.
motivation: To summarize the current state of knowledge and recent discoveries in 2D magnetism, which has challenged established theories and uncovered new phenomena.
method: The paper is a review that surveys experimental and theoretical progress in 2D van der Waals magnets, including topics like topology, quantum dynamics, Floquet effects, magnons, and spintronics.
result: The review highlights the rapid evolution of the field, expanding theoretical understanding, materials capabilities, and experimental phenomenology.
conclusion: The field of 2D van der Waals magnets is actively evolving and opening new directions for applications.

title: Kagome Metals
authors: Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, And Stephen D. Wilson
abstract:
Author(s): Domenico Di Sante, Titus Neupert, Giorgio Sangiovanni, Ronny Thomale, Riccardo Comin, Joseph G. Checkelsky, Ilija Zeljkovic, and Stephen D. Wilson

The kagome lattice is a two-dimensional tiling of hexagons and triangles named after a Japanese basket weaving technique. Its geometry gives rise to highly frustrated interactions and interference effects experienced by electrons and their multiple degrees of freedom. In metals, the exploration of materials with kagome conduction networks is driven by predictions of realizing new electronic states where these interference effects are dominant, amplifying electronic interactions and many-body effects. In these kagome metals, these amplified correlation effects in combination with spin-orbit coupling and other forms of frustration have given rise to a wealth of phenomena beyond expectations. These include unusual states and responses born from topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, sublattice interference effects at saddle points such as unconventional superconductivity, orbital antiferromagnetism and flux phases, amplified anomalous Hall effects, and electronic nematic states. This review examines the theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, with the aim of elucidating fundamental mechanisms underlying the observed exotic phenomena.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015002] Published Thu Feb 12, 2026.
tldr: A review of kagome metals, focusing on exotic electronic states arising from geometric frustration and interference effects.
motivation: To understand the fundamental mechanisms behind unusual phenomena observed in kagome metals, such as unconventional superconductivity and topological flat bands.
method: The paper reviews theoretical and experimental work on kagome metals, synthesizing findings from multiple studies.
result: Kagome metals exhibit a wealth of exotic states including topological flat bands, massive Dirac fermions, unconventional superconductivity, and orbital antiferromagnetism.
conclusion: The kagome lattice provides a rich platform for exploring correlated electron physics and may lead to new quantum states of matter.

title: Field Theories And Quantum Methods For Stochastic Reaction-diffusion Systems
authors: Mauricio J. Del Razo, Tommaso Lamma, And Wout Merbis
abstract:
Author(s): Mauricio J. del Razo, Tommaso Lamma, and Wout Merbis

The exchange of energy and molecules in a living cell, the spread of opinions through a society, and the flow of traffic in a crowded city are very different phenomena, yet they are all examples of complex systems composed of many agents that interact with each other and exchange energy or particles with the environment. These systems can be modeled as stochastic reaction-diffusion systems. In this pedagogical review, the authors apply powerful field-theoretic methods to these systems, unifying diverse approaches under a single framework. The methods are useful for handling chemical systems but also have applications in a wide range of areas such as ecology and epidemiology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 015001] Published Thu Jan 22, 2026.
tldr: A pedagogical review applying field-theoretic methods to stochastic reaction-diffusion systems, with applications in chemistry, ecology, and epidemiology.
motivation: Stochastic reaction-diffusion systems model many complex systems, but a unified framework is lacking.
method: The authors review field-theoretic methods, including path integrals and Doi-Peliti formalism, to treat these systems.
result: The review unifies diverse approaches and demonstrates applications in chemical, ecological, and epidemiological contexts.
conclusion: Field-theoretic methods provide a powerful and unifying framework for analyzing stochastic reaction-diffusion systems.

title: Spin-glass Dynamics: Experiment, Theory, And Simulation
authors: E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, And D. Yllanes
abstract:
Author(s): E. D. Dahlberg, I. González-Adalid Pemartín, E. Marinari, G. Parisi, F. Ricci-Tersenghi, V. Martin-Mayor, J. Moreno-Gordo, R. L. Orbach, I. Paga, J. J. Ruiz-Lorenzo, and D. Yllanes

This review updates the field of spin glasses with broad application to a large variety of physical systems. In particular, this review tracks the progress of experiment, theory, and large-scale simulations. It highlights the importance of their synergy, from the inception of the field to the present day, and includes future opportunities for research.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045005] Published Mon Dec 15, 2025.
tldr: A review of spin-glass dynamics covering experiment, theory, and simulation.
motivation: To provide an updated overview of spin-glass research and highlight the synergy between experiment, theory, and simulation.
method: Review of experimental, theoretical, and computational studies of spin glasses.
result: Summarizes progress in understanding spin-glass dynamics and identifies future research opportunities.
conclusion: Spin-glass dynamics remain a rich field with broad applications, and continued interdisciplinary collaboration is essential.

title: Kitaev Quantum Spin Liquids
authors: Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, And Hae-Young Kee
abstract:
Author(s): Yuji Matsuda, Takasada Shibauchi, and Hae-Young Kee

Frustration in spin systems can prevent ordering even at =0, creating quantum spin liquids that have been sought since Anderson’s pioneering work in 1973 and his influential 1987 paper connecting them to high-temperature superconductivity. Kitaev’s solvable spin-1/2 models on a honeycomb lattice brought renewed attention to this field, with Jackeli and Khaliullin later revealing how to engineer Kitaev interactions in real materials. This review highlights theoretical and experimental developments in Kitaev spin liquids, emphasizing leading candidate materials and their broad topological properties such as chiral edge modes. Consequently, it provides essential insights for both experimentalists and theorists working on quantum spin liquid problems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045003] Published Wed Dec 03, 2025.
tldr: A review of Kitaev quantum spin liquids, focusing on candidate materials and topological properties.
motivation: Quantum spin liquids are exotic states of matter with potential applications in quantum computing, but the paper focuses on condensed matter physics rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: The review summarizes theoretical models (Kitaev honeycomb model) and experimental progress in candidate materials.
result: Key topological properties such as chiral edge modes are discussed, but no new results are presented.
conclusion: The paper provides a comprehensive overview for researchers in condensed matter physics, but does not directly address quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: The Ups And Downs Of Internal Conversion
authors: Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, And Salvy P. Russo
abstract:
Author(s): Anjay Manian, Zifei Chen, Hugh T. Sullivan, and Salvy P. Russo

This review examines the theoretical methods used to describe the photophysical process of internal conversion in quantum systems. These models explore all facets of the nonradiative mechanism, and the review presents an outlook on how they can be incorporated in studies relevant to applications, for example, in photonics and energy harvesting.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 035003] Published Tue Sep 16, 2025.
tldr: A review of theoretical methods for internal conversion in quantum systems, with applications in photonics and energy harvesting.
motivation: Internal conversion is a key nonradiative process in molecular systems, and understanding its theoretical underpinnings is important for applications like photonics and energy harvesting.
method: The paper reviews various theoretical models describing internal conversion, including nonradiative mechanisms and their incorporation into application-relevant studies.
result: The review summarizes the current state of theoretical methods for internal conversion and provides an outlook for future research.
conclusion: Theoretical methods for internal conversion are diverse and can be applied to photonics and energy harvesting, but the paper does not present new results or directly advance quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Colloquium: Quantum Properties And Functionalities Of Magnetic Skyrmions
authors: Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, And Christos Panagopoulos
abstract:
Author(s): Alexander P. Petrović, Christina Psaroudaki, Peter Fischer, Markus Garst, and Christos Panagopoulos

Skyrmions are topological field configurations that were first discussed in the context of high-energy theory. In recent years, skyrmionic spin patterns in solid-state systems have received much attention, in part for their promising application potential. This Colloquium discusses quantum-mechanical aspects of such magnetic skyrmions, both for the interactions that underlie skyrmion formation and for quantum features of the skyrmions themselves.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 031001] Published Tue Jul 08, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews quantum properties and functionalities of magnetic skyrmions, focusing on their formation and quantum features.
motivation: Magnetic skyrmions are promising for spintronic applications, and understanding their quantum aspects could enable new functionalities.
method: The paper reviews theoretical and experimental work on skyrmion formation, quantum tunneling, and quantum-classical correspondence.
result: It highlights quantum effects such as skyrmion tunneling and the role of quantum fluctuations in skyrmion stability.
conclusion: Quantum skyrmions may offer novel functionalities for future quantum technologies, but the field is still developing.

title: Spin-dependent Exotic Interactions
authors: Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, And Dmitry Budker
abstract:
Author(s): Lei Cong, Wei Ji, Pavel Fadeev, Filip Ficek, Min Jiang, Victor V. Flambaum, Haosen Guan, Derek F. Jackson Kimball, Mikhail G. Kozlov, Yevgeny V. Stadnik, and Dmitry Budker

This review presents a comprehensive summary of theoretical investigations and experimental searches for spin-dependent interactions beyond the standard model. These interactions may be mediated by various types of exotic bosons, and their existence and properties may, in turn, explain the nature of dark matter and dark energy. The described experiments also probe the discrete fundamental symmetries of nature.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 025005] Published Tue Jun 24, 2025.
tldr: A comprehensive review of theoretical and experimental searches for spin-dependent exotic interactions beyond the standard model, including their possible connection to dark matter and dark energy.
motivation: To understand the nature of dark matter and dark energy and to test fundamental symmetries of nature through spin-dependent interactions mediated by exotic bosons.
method: The paper reviews a wide range of theoretical models and experimental techniques, including atomic magnetometry, torsion balances, and precision spectroscopy, used to search for spin-dependent forces.
result: The review summarizes current experimental constraints on various spin-dependent interactions and discusses future prospects for improved sensitivity.
conclusion: Spin-dependent exotic interactions remain a promising avenue for discovering new physics, but no definitive evidence has been found; further experimental and theoretical work is needed.

title: Colloquium: Materials That Exceed Classical Thermodynamic Bounds On Properties
authors: Roderic S. Lakes
abstract:
Author(s): Roderic S. Lakes

Classical thermodynamic bounds provide constraints on values that are expected in measurements of certain physical properties. In a variety of fields, some measurements exceed these bounds. This apparent violation of thermodynamics arises because the measurements are made in ways that violate the underlying assumptions made when deriving these bounds. This Colloquium describes a wide variety of circumstances where such violations occur and which of the underlying assumptions are violated in each case. It also describes how interesting material properties can be developed using materials designed to violate these assumptions.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 021002] Published Wed May 14, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews materials that appear to exceed classical thermodynamic bounds on properties, explaining the violations by examining underlying assumptions.
motivation: Classical thermodynamic bounds are often assumed to be fundamental, but many measurements exceed them; understanding why can lead to novel materials.
method: The paper surveys a wide variety of circumstances where measured properties exceed classical bounds and identifies which assumptions are violated in each case.
result: It shows that apparent violations arise because measurements are made in ways that violate the assumptions behind the bounds, not because thermodynamics is wrong.
conclusion: Materials can be designed to exploit violations of these assumptions to achieve properties that surpass classical thermodynamic limits.

title: Colloquium: Synthetic Quantum Matter In Nonstandard Geometries
authors: Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, And Christof Weitenberg
abstract:
Author(s): Tobias Grass, Dario Bercioux, Utso Bhattacharya, Maciej Lewenstein, Hai Son Nguyen, and Christof Weitenberg

This Colloquium presents ways to implement fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions in atomic, photonic, and electronic systems. The study of quantum many-body physics in these exotic geometries permits simulation of phenomena from topology in condensed matter to models of gravity and cosmology.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 011001] Published Tue Mar 25, 2025.
tldr: This Colloquium reviews experimental and theoretical approaches to realizing quantum many-body systems in fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher dimensions.
motivation: To explore exotic geometries that enable simulation of phenomena from condensed matter topology to gravity and cosmology.
method: Survey of atomic, photonic, and electronic platforms for implementing nonstandard geometries, including synthetic dimensions and curved spaces.
result: Summarizes recent progress in engineering fractal lattices, curved spaces, and higher-dimensional systems, highlighting key experimental demonstrations.
conclusion: These synthetic quantum matter platforms open new avenues for studying fundamental physics but are not directly aligned with the user's core research directions.

title: Self-aligning Polar Active Matter
authors: Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, And Amir Shee
abstract:
Author(s): Paul Baconnier, Olivier Dauchot, Vincent Démery, Gustavo Düring, Silke Henkes, Cristián Huepe, and Amir Shee

What if active units could align–or even antialign–their orientation with their own velocity? This intriguing self-alignment property unlocks a spectrum of fascinating behaviors, from single self-propelled particles orbiting in harmonic traps to transformative collective phenomena like synchronized motion in dense or solid elastic assemblies. Unlike systems where units simply mimic their neighbors, self-alignment fundamentally reshapes how motion emerges, paving the way for groundbreaking discoveries in biology, smart materials, and robotics. This review uncovers the hidden power of self-alignment in active systems, introduces a unified mathematical and conceptual framework, explores existing models of self-alignment, and highlights its transformative impact on the study and real-world applications of active systems.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015007] Published Thu Mar 20, 2025.
tldr: A review of self-alignment in polar active matter, focusing on collective motion in biological and robotic systems.
motivation: To understand how self-alignment of active units with their velocity leads to novel collective behaviors, with applications in biology, smart materials, and robotics.
method: The paper reviews existing models and experiments on self-alignment in active matter, presenting a unified mathematical and conceptual framework.
result: Self-alignment enables phenomena such as orbiting in harmonic traps and synchronized motion in dense assemblies, fundamentally reshaping emergent motion.
conclusion: Self-alignment is a key mechanism in active matter that opens new avenues for research and applications in active systems.

title: Massive Quantum Systems As Interfaces Of Quantum Mechanics And Gravity
authors: Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, And Clara C. Wanjura
abstract:
Author(s): Sougato Bose, Ivette Fuentes, Andrew A. Geraci, Saba Mehsar Khan, Sofia Qvarfort, Markus Rademacher, Muddassar Rashid, Marko Toroš, Hendrik Ulbricht, and Clara C. Wanjura

The authors review theories and experimental state-of-the-art efforts to study the effects of gravity on massive quantum systems. Classical gravity is the least precisely tested natural force and may be addressed via precision quantum probes. Experiments testing whether the quantum nature of gravity causes decoherence and collapse of matter-wave functions and whether it can mediate entanglement between separate massive particles are underway, and their results will guide the theoretical description of gravity effects on a laboratory scale.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 015003] Published Thu Feb 13, 2025.
tldr: A review of theoretical and experimental efforts to study gravity's effects on massive quantum systems, including tests of quantum gravity and entanglement mediated by gravity.
motivation: Classical gravity is the least precisely tested natural force, and massive quantum systems may serve as probes to study gravity's quantum nature.
method: The paper reviews theories of gravity-induced decoherence, collapse models, and entanglement generation, along with experimental platforms such as matter-wave interferometry and optomechanics.
result: Current experiments are testing whether gravity causes decoherence or can mediate entanglement between massive particles, with results guiding future theoretical descriptions.
conclusion: Massive quantum systems provide a promising avenue to explore the interface between quantum mechanics and gravity, but the field is still in early stages.

title: On The Significance Of Wigner’s Friend In Contexts Beyond Quantum Foundations
authors: Caroline L. Jones And Markus P. Mueller
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2147 (2026).

There has been a surge of recent interest in the Wigner's Friend paradox, sparking several novel thought experiments and no-go theorems. The main narrative has been that Wigner's Friend highlights a counterintuitive feature that is unique to quantum theory, and which is closely related to the quantum measurement problem. Here, we challenge this view. We argue that the gist of the Wigner's Friend paradox can be reproduced without assuming quantum physics, and that it underlies a much broader class of enigmas in the foundations of physics and philosophy. To show this, we first consider several recently proposed Extended Wigner's Friend scenarios, and demonstrate that some of their implications for the absoluteness of observations can be reproduced by classical thought experiments that involve the duplication of agents. Crucially, some of these classical scenarios are technologically much easier to implement than their quantum counterparts. Then, we argue that the essential structural ingredient of all these scenarios is a feature that we call "Restriction A": that a physical theory cannot give us a probabilistic description of the observations of all agents. Finally, we argue that this difficulty is at the core of other puzzles in the foundations of physics and philosophy, and demonstrate this explicitly for cosmology's Boltzmann brain problem. Our analysis suggests that Wigner's Friend should be studied in a larger context, addressing a frontier of human knowledge beyond quantum foundations: to obtain reliable predictions for experiments in which these predictions can be privately but not intersubjectively verified.

.
tldr: The paper argues that the Wigner's Friend paradox is not unique to quantum theory and can be reproduced classically, suggesting broader implications for foundations of physics and philosophy.
motivation: Recent interest in Wigner's Friend paradox has focused on quantum foundations, but the authors challenge this view by showing the paradox can arise without quantum physics.
method: The authors analyze Extended Wigner's Friend scenarios and construct classical thought experiments with agent duplication to demonstrate that the core issue, termed 'Restriction A', is a general feature of physical theories.
result: They show that some implications of Wigner's Friend scenarios can be reproduced classically, and that the underlying difficulty applies to other puzzles like the Boltzmann brain problem.
conclusion: Wigner's Friend should be studied in a broader context beyond quantum foundations, addressing challenges in obtaining reliable predictions when observations are privately but not intersubjectively verifiable.

title: Qubit Operations Using A Modular Optical System Engineered With PyOpticL: A code-to-CAD Optical Layout Tool
authors: Jacob Myers, Christopher Caron, Nishat Helaly, Zhenyu Wei, Justin Oh, Zack Gotobed, Kotaro Yabe, And Robert J. Niffenegger
abstract:
Quantum 10, 2135 (2026).

Complex optical design is hindered by conventional piecewise setup, which prevents modularization and therefore abstraction of subsystems at the circuit level. This limits multiple fields that require complex optics systems, including quantum computing with atoms and trapped ions, because their optical systems are not scalable. We present an open-source Python library for optical layout (PyOpticL) which uses beam-path simulation and dynamic beam-path routing for quick and easy optical layout by placing optical elements along the beam path without a priori specification, enabling adaptive, path-based layouts with automatic routing and connectivity. We use PyOpticL to create modular `drop-in' optical baseplates for common optical subsystems used in atomic and molecular optics (AMO) experiments including laser sources, frequency and intensity modulation, and locking to an atomic reference for stabilization. We demonstrate this minimal working example of a dynamic full laser system for strontium trapped ions by using it for laser cooling, qubit state detection, and over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates with 3D printed baseplates. This enables a new paradigm of design abstraction layers for engineering optical systems leveraging modular baseplates, as they can be used for any wavelength in the system and enables scaling up the underlying optical systems for quantum computers. This new open-source hardware and software code-to-CAD library seeks to foster open-source collaborative hardware and systems design across numerous fields of research including AMO physics and quantum computing with neutral atoms and trapped ions.

.
tldr: This paper presents an open-source Python library for optical layout (PyOpticL) and demonstrates its use for building modular optical systems for trapped-ion quantum computing.
motivation: Complex optical design in quantum computing with atoms and trapped ions is hindered by conventional piecewise setup, which prevents modularization and scalability.
method: The authors developed PyOpticL, a Python library that uses beam-path simulation and dynamic routing to enable adaptive, path-based layouts. They created modular 'drop-in' optical baseplates for common subsystems and demonstrated a full laser system for strontium trapped ions.
result: The system achieved over 99% fidelity single-qubit gates and was used for laser cooling and qubit state detection, demonstrating the viability of the modular approach.
conclusion: PyOpticL enables a new paradigm of design abstraction layers for engineering optical systems, fostering open-source collaborative hardware design for AMO physics and quantum computing.

title: Sorting Prolate And Oblate Spheroids With A Diatomic Gas In A Magnetic Field
authors: Ruben Lier
abstract: For a gas of diatomic particles with a nonzero magnetic moment, the Senftleben–Beenakker effect implies that transport can be affected by a magnetic field even when the particles are charge neutral. In such a gas, two independent anisotropic odd viscosities are allowed by symmetry and can have opposite signs. We study the resulting odd-viscous Stokes flow around spheroids in the regime where the odd viscosities are small compared to the shear viscosity. Using a perturbative expansion around the spherical solution and the Lorentz reciprocal theorem, we compute the lift forces on oblate and prolate spheroids for general values of the two odd viscosity coefficients. We show that the resulting Hall angles can differ for oblate and prolate spheroids, implying that sedimentation in a diatomic gas subject to a background magnetic field can separate particles according to shape.
tldr: This paper studies odd-viscous Stokes flow around spheroids in a diatomic gas under a magnetic field, showing shape-based separation via Hall angles.
motivation: Understanding how magnetic fields affect transport in neutral diatomic gases (Senftleben-Beenakker effect) and exploiting odd viscosities for particle separation.
method: Perturbative expansion around spherical solution and Lorentz reciprocal theorem to compute lift forces on oblate and prolate spheroids for general odd viscosity coefficients.
result: Hall angles differ for oblate and prolate spheroids, enabling shape-based separation during sedimentation in a magnetic field.
conclusion: The study demonstrates a mechanism to separate particles by shape using odd viscosities in a diatomic gas under a magnetic field.

title: Gravitational And Other Shifts Of Whispering-gallery And Gravitational State Interference Patterns Of Light Neutral Particles
authors: V V Nesvizhevsky, J A Pioquinto, K Schreiner, S Baeßler, P Crivelli, F Nez, S Reynaud, P Yzombard, S A Vasiliev And E Widmann
abstract: We discuss the interference patterns of gravitational and whispering gallery quantum states that can be observed with neutrons, atoms, antiatoms, muonium (Mu), positronium (Ps), and other light neutral particles. A gravitational shift of interference patterns of neutron gravitational and whispering-gallery states can be easily observed with cold, very cold, or ultracold neutrons. The developed methods can be used for observing/searching for other shifts in fundamental neutron physics experiments, for instance, for measuring the gravitational constant or constraining the neutron electric charge. A series of such measurements will be made with neutrons at the PF1B, PF2, D17 facilities at the ILL. A peculiar feature of analogous atomic (anti-atomic) experiments is the much smaller effective critical energies of the materials of mirrors for (anti)atoms. We evaluated parameters that make a measurement of the hydrogen and antihydrogen whispering-gallery states and their gravitational shifts feasible. A series of such measurements will be made with hydrogen and deuterium atoms by the GRASIAN collaboration in Vienna and Turku. A similar measurement with antihydrogen atoms may be of interest for the GBAR experiment, the ASACUSA experiment, which is producing a beam of slow antihydrogen atoms, and other experiments at CERN that study the gravitational properties of antimatter. Quantum reflection (QR) of Mu and Ps from material surfaces opens the possibility of observing whispering-gallery states, although such measurements remain experimentally challenging. Because of the small masses of Mu and Ps, their effective critical energies of the mirror materials are much higher for them than the effective critical energies for hydrogen and other atoms. The observation of gravitational shifts of such states is particularly demanding because of the extremely short lifetimes of these systems. Measurements of whispering gallery states with all these atoms and particles yield precise and detailed information on the QR properties of materials, providing valuable input for both fundamental physics and surface physics studies.
tldr: This paper discusses gravitational and whispering-gallery state interference patterns for light neutral particles, focusing on experimental measurements of gravitational shifts and quantum reflection.
motivation: To explore gravitational and other shifts in interference patterns of quantum states of neutrons, atoms, and antiatoms, which could provide tests of fundamental physics and surface properties.
method: The authors analyze the feasibility of observing gravitational and whispering-gallery states for various particles (neutrons, hydrogen, antihydrogen, muonium, positronium) using existing and proposed experimental setups.
result: Gravitational shifts can be easily observed with neutrons; hydrogen and antihydrogen experiments are feasible; muonium and positronium measurements are challenging due to short lifetimes.
conclusion: These measurements can yield precise information on quantum reflection and fundamental constants, but the paper is primarily experimental and phenomenological, not advancing quantum information or thermodynamics theory.

title: Readjustment Of Intrinsic Activity Parameters Governs The Rectified Transport In Asymmetric Ratchets
authors: Yunyan Chen, Xiaoyuan Yu, Fengguo Li And Baoquan Ai
abstract: The rectified transport of active Brownian particles (ABPs) in asymmetric ratchets has been extensively studied. However, most existing literature regulates rectification by designing different structural boundaries. In this work, we shift the research perspective to the internal properties of ABPs and explore the influence of their internal physical parameters on the transport process. Using the vibration-driven vehicle (VDV) as a macroscopic experimental model for ABPs, we systematically adjust the overall mass and position of center of mass of the VDV to reveal its underlying dynamic mechanism. Through long-time dynamic tracking, we identify a ‘parameters readjustment effect’: an increase in mass weakens the particle’s average velocity and persistence length, ultimately driving the active system into a noise-dominated macroscopic localized state. More importantly, the shift of the center of mass induces persistent translational–rotational coupling in the VDV, leading to an anomalous non-monotonic reentrant phase transition in the rectification probability of the system. Our study reveals that this anomalous transport law is fundamentally governed by the dynamic spatial competition between the intrinsic chiral orbit radius of the VDV and the geometric characteristic scale of the channel. Coarse-grained ABP numerical simulations reproduce the overall experimental trends. This work indicates that load-induced parameters evolution is not merely a physical perturbation, but a core dimension that determines macroscopic transport behavior, providing physical insights and principles for going beyond purely geometric design constraints and designing efficient active rectification systems.
tldr: This paper studies how internal parameters of active Brownian particles affect rectified transport in asymmetric ratchets, using a macroscopic experimental model.
motivation: Most existing work on active ratchets focuses on structural boundaries; this work shifts to internal properties like mass and center of mass position.
method: A vibration-driven vehicle serves as a macroscopic analog of active Brownian particles; mass and center of mass are systematically varied, and long-time dynamics are tracked experimentally and via coarse-grained simulations.
result: Increasing mass reduces average velocity and persistence length, leading to a noise-dominated localized state; shifting the center of mass induces a non-monotonic reentrant phase transition in rectification probability.
conclusion: Load-induced parameter evolution is a core determinant of macroscopic transport behavior, offering design principles beyond geometric constraints.

title: Chiral Graviton Modes In Fermionic Fractional Chern Insulators
authors: Min Long, Zeno Bacciconi, Hongyu Lu, Hernan B Xavier, Zi Yang Meng And Marcello Dalmonte
abstract: Chiral graviton modes are hallmark collective excitations of fractional quantum Hall (FQH) liquids. However, their existence on the lattice, where continuum symmetries that protect them from decay are lost, is still an open and urgent question, especially considering the recent advances in the realization of fractional Chern insulators (FCI) in transition metal dichalcogenides and rhombohedral pentalayer graphene. Here we present a comprehensive theoretical and numerical study of graviton-modes in fermionic FCI, and thoroughly demonstrate their existence. We first derive a lattice stress tensor operator in the context of the fermionic Harper–Hofstadter (HH) model which captures the graviton in the flat band limit. Importantly, we discover that such lattice stress-tensor operators are deeply connected to correlation hole dynamics, readily generalizable to generic Chern bands. We then explicitly show the adiabatic connection between FQH and FCI chiral graviton modes by interpolating from a low flux HH model to a Checkerboard lattice model that hosts a topological flat band. In particular, using state-of-the-art matrix product state and exact diagonalization simulations, we provide strong evidence that chiral graviton modes are long-lived excitations in FCIs despite the lack of continuous symmetries and the scattering with a two-magnetoroton continuum. By means of a careful finite-size analysis, we show that the lattice generates an intrinsic decay rate for the graviton mode which is small compared to its energy. We discuss the relevance of our results for the exploration of graviton modes in FCI phases realized in solid state settings, experimental utility on diagnosis of fractional topological phases, as well as cold atom experiments.
tldr: This paper studies chiral graviton modes in fractional Chern insulators, a topic in condensed matter physics with no direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
motivation: To determine whether chiral graviton modes, hallmark excitations of fractional quantum Hall liquids, exist in lattice fractional Chern insulators where continuum symmetries are absent.
method: Derives a lattice stress tensor operator for the Harper-Hofstadter model and uses matrix product state and exact diagonalization simulations to study graviton modes in a checkerboard lattice model.
result: Provides evidence that chiral graviton modes are long-lived excitations in FCIs despite lack of continuous symmetries, with a small intrinsic decay rate compared to energy.
conclusion: The results are relevant for exploring graviton modes in solid-state and cold-atom experiments, but the paper does not address quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Vortex Solitons In Disclination Quasicrystals
authors: Hua Zhong, Yaroslav V Kartashov, Yongdong Li, Fangwei Ye And Yiqi Zhang
abstract: Quasicrystals are ubiquitous in nature. They represent unique aperiodic materials featuring long-range order that occupy an intermediate niche between exactly periodic and disordered materials. These properties are reflected in the unusual evolutionary dynamics of excitations and unique localization properties of linear eigenmodes supported by quasicrystals. In particular, being the structures characterized by discrete rotational symmetry of order , photonic quasicrystals can support the stable propagation of linear vortex-carrying light beams and vortex solitons. However, the impact of discrete rotational symmetry of quasicrystals on the properties of vortex light states has not been investigated so far, as only the systems constructed using the simplest Penrose tiling or corresponding optically induced Penrose lattices are considered in this context. Here, we propose a broad class of quasicrystals with global topological defects—disclinations—introduced into their structure that allows to produce novel quasicrystalline structures with any desired order of discrete rotational symmetry from the basic Penrose structure. Such global topological deformation substantially enriches the linear spectrum of quasicrystals, allowing them to support new types of linear vortex states and bifurcating from them families of stable thresholdless vortex solitons with unusual intensity and phase distributions. We find two different classes of stable vortex solitons comprising in-phase or out-of-phase pairs of closely located bright spots, with total intensity distribution reflecting a particular discrete rotational symmetry of the quasicrystal with disclination. Remarkably, even low-charge vortex solitons can be stable in quasicrystals with disclinations, whereas stability intervals for them broaden with the decrease of the discrete rotational symmetry of quasicrystals. Our results extend the theory of localization in quasicrystals to structures with global topological deformation, highlighting emerging prospects for the robust transmission of power or information arising in these systems.
tldr: This paper studies vortex solitons in photonic quasicrystals with disclinations, focusing on their stability and intensity distributions.
motivation: To understand how global topological defects (disclinations) in quasicrystals affect the properties of vortex light states, which have not been investigated before.
method: The authors propose a class of quasicrystals with disclinations, analyze their linear spectrum, and numerically find families of stable vortex solitons.
result: Two classes of stable vortex solitons are found, with stability intervals broadening as discrete rotational symmetry decreases.
conclusion: The results extend localization theory to quasicrystals with topological deformations, offering potential for robust transmission of power or information.

title: Uniaxial-stress-induced Magnetic Transitions In The Triangular-lattice Antiferromagnet PdCrO2
authors: Nina Stilkerich, Tobias Ritschel, Hilary M L Noad, Richard Waite, Dmitry Khalyavin, Kousuke Ishida, Pascal Manuel, Fabio Orlandi, Seunghyun Khim, Elena Gati, Andrew P Mackenzie, Jochen Geck And Clifford W Hicks
abstract: Uniaxial stress is a promising method to tune magnetic frustration, allowing its effects to be studied in a precise way. In this work, uniaxial stress is applied to the triangular-lattice antiferromagnet PdCrO . The Cr–Cr magnetic interaction is very sensitive to interatomic separation, so laboratory-achievable stress can induce substantial changes in magnetic structure. Results from three types of measurement are presented: x-ray diffraction, the stress–strain relationship, and neutron diffraction. The combined data show that the elastic moduli of PdCrO are strongly affected by stress-induced changes in magnetic structure. A new, first-order stress-induced magnetic transition is observed, at which the lattice constant shrinks by 0.21%. The lattice stiffens dramatically across this transition: the Young’s modulus increases by GPa, and the Poisson ratio falls from to . This stiffening indicates that the magnetic order ‘locks,’ that is, becomes insensitive to lattice strain. This locking might occur because the new stress-induced magnetic order nests the Fermi surface of the Pd sheets. Other frustrated magnets, including candidate spin liquids, may show similarly strong coupling between magnetic and elastic degrees of freedom.
tldr: This paper studies stress-induced magnetic transitions in the triangular-lattice antiferromagnet PdCrO2, focusing on the coupling between magnetic order and elastic properties.
motivation: To understand how uniaxial stress can tune magnetic frustration and induce new magnetic phases in frustrated magnets.
method: Combined x-ray diffraction, stress-strain measurements, and neutron diffraction under uniaxial stress.
result: A first-order stress-induced magnetic transition is observed, accompanied by a 0.21% lattice shrinkage and dramatic stiffening of the lattice.
conclusion: The magnetic order becomes locked under stress, likely due to Fermi surface nesting, suggesting strong magnetoelastic coupling in frustrated magnets.

title: Defect Approach To Giant Graviton Dynamics
authors: Yunfeng Jiang And Xinan Zhou Junding Chen
abstract: We develop a framework of zero dimensional defects for analyzing light–light–heavy–heavy (LLHH) correlators in conformal field theories. We specifically apply this formalism to correlators of giant gravitons in super Yang–Mills to probe the nontrivial physics beyond planarity. By combining this framework with bootstrap techniques, we compute all four-point functions at strong coupling involving two maximal giant gravitons and two supergravitons of arbitrary dimensions. We identify a partially broken, higher-dimensional hidden symmetry—a defect extension of 10d hidden conformal symmetry–present at both strong and weak coupling, which allows these correlators to be packaged into a single generating function. Furthermore, we perform a systematic OPE analysis of the strong-coupling correlators, extracting the complete spectrum of anomalous dimensions for the defect-channel double-particle operators. Finally, we argue that the defect perspective provides the natural nonperturbative description for any LLHH correlator by showing that four-point conformal blocks reduce to defect two-point blocks in the heavy limit.
tldr: This paper develops a defect framework for computing LLHH correlators in conformal field theories, applied to giant gravitons in super Yang-Mills theory.
motivation: To understand non-planar corrections in AdS/CFT by studying correlators involving heavy operators like giant gravitons.
method: Combines zero-dimensional defect formalism with bootstrap techniques to compute four-point functions at strong coupling.
result: Identifies a hidden 10d conformal symmetry and extracts the full spectrum of anomalous dimensions for defect-channel operators.
conclusion: The defect perspective provides a natural nonperturbative description for LLHH correlators in the heavy limit.

title: Direct Visualization Of Field-driven Valence Band Modulation In Electrostatically Reconfigured Graphene Devices
authors: Umidakhon Rayimjonova, Chin-Yi Huang, Yi-Cheng Weng, Elin Cartwright, Fredrik O L Johansson, Noemi Vannucchi, Pavel Dudin, Avila Jose, Pei Ding, David Muradas-Belinchón, Henry Nameirakpam, Zhaojun Li, Andreas Lindblad And M Venkata Kamalakar
abstract: Graphene with ultrathin metal-oxide layers has emerged as a scalable platform for integrated electronic, spintronic, and neuromorphic devices. The in-plane electric fields in such devices are typically inferred indirectly from transport measurements, which do not provide microscopic details of the interface potential profile. Here, we use photoemission microscopy to uncover the precise electrostatic landscape of a complete device comprising diverse, heterogeneous ultrathin metal-oxide-covered graphene junctions. Using in operando x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy with submicron resolution, we directly image the real potential profile across an entire graphene device, including regions covered by AlOx and TiOx nanometer-thick overlayers. Tracking the valence band edge under current bias and gate voltage enables quantitative analysis of internal field evolution via a spectroscopic screening factor, revealing an up to more than 50% suppression of the electric field in graphene covered with oxides, in agreement with transport measurements. This demonstrates local reconfiguration of electric fields in graphene for advanced two-dimensional (2D) device engineering and circuitry, while our operando circuit spectroscopy measurements provide a generic means to uncover intricate potential landscapes and carrier redistribution in 2D electronic and spintronic circuits.
tldr: This paper uses photoemission microscopy to directly visualize the electrostatic potential profile in graphene devices with oxide overlayers, revealing field suppression.
motivation: Understanding the microscopic electrostatic landscape in graphene devices is crucial for optimizing electronic and spintronic performance, but indirect transport measurements lack spatial detail.
method: The authors employ in operando x-ray photoelectron spectroscopy with submicron resolution to image the valence band edge across a graphene device under bias and gate voltage, extracting a spectroscopic screening factor.
result: They observe up to 50% suppression of the electric field in graphene regions covered by AlOx and TiOx, consistent with transport measurements.
conclusion: Operando circuit spectroscopy provides a generic method to map potential landscapes in 2D devices, enabling advanced engineering of graphene-based circuits.

tldr: This paper applies superstatistics to model circulation fluctuations in fluid turbulence, a topic in classical nonequilibrium statistical mechanics.
motivation: Understanding the statistical nature of fluid turbulence is a long-standing challenge in nonequilibrium statistical mechanics.
method: The authors use a superstatistics approach, which models fluctuations as a mixture of Gaussian distributions with varying parameters, to analyze turbulent circulation data.
result: They provide evidence that superstatistics accurately captures the heavy-tailed probability distributions observed in turbulent circulation fluctuations.

title: Data-driven Discovery Of Dynamical Models In Biology
authors: Bartosz Prokop
Lendert Gelens
abstract: Nature Reviews Physics, Published online: 25 June 2026;
tldr: This paper reviews data-driven methods for discovering dynamical models in biology, focusing on regression, network architectures, and decomposition techniques.
motivation: Biological systems are complex and often lack first-principles models, motivating the use of data-driven approaches to infer dynamics from time-resolved data.
method: The authors compare regression-based methods, network-based architectures, and decomposition techniques, evaluating their strengths and limitations for extracting dynamical information.
result: The review highlights the complementarity of different approaches and provides guidance on selecting methods based on data characteristics and biological questions.
conclusion: Data-driven discovery is a powerful tool for modeling biological dynamics, but careful method selection and validation are crucial.

abstract:

[Phys. Rev. Lett. 137, 021804] Published Fri Jul 10, 2026.
tldr: This paper uses historical Cavendish-type experiments to set new bounds on millicharged particles.
motivation: Millicharged particles are hypothetical particles with a tiny fraction of the electron's charge, and their existence is constrained by various experiments. The authors aim to leverage old Cavendish experiments to improve these constraints.
method: The authors reinterpret data from classic Cavendish torsion balance experiments, which measure the electrostatic force between charged objects, to derive limits on the charge of millicharged particles.
result: New upper bounds on the charge of millicharged particles are obtained, improving upon previous constraints for certain mass ranges.
conclusion: The study demonstrates that historical experiments can still provide valuable constraints on new physics, specifically for millicharged particles.

conclusion: Vibrational entropy plays a crucial role in stabilizing polar surfaces, which has implications for understanding surface properties in catalysis and electronics.

title: Inferring The Underlying Higher-order Network Structure From Low-resolution Interaction State Data
authors: Chuang Ma, Xiao-Feng Luo, Rui-Hui He, Dao-Yu Li, Hai-Feng Zhang And Gui-Quan Sun
abstract: Network reconstruction aims to infer the underlying interactions between entities from observed data and serves as a cornerstone of network science. While most existing methods focus on dynamics-based data and primarily target binary interactions, real-world data often reflect coarse-grained interaction states of individuals over specific time intervals and may involve complex multi-body interactions beyond pairwise connections. Reconstructing the underlying higher-order network structure from such low-resolution interaction state data is therefore of critical importance. In this paper, we formulate an optimization model for inferring higher-order structures based on the minimum description length principle. To solve this problem, we propose a Bayesian network reconstruction method that integrates distribution estimation with Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling. Our method begins by generating candidate configurations for each time interval via MCMC sampling, then constructs a Bayesian network—guided by minimum-entropy—to capture dependencies between configurations across different time intervals. Finally, an iterative update strategy based on distribution estimation is employed to approach the optimal solution. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method.
tldr: This paper proposes a method to infer higher-order network structures from low-resolution interaction state data using Bayesian networks and MCMC sampling.
motivation: Existing network reconstruction methods focus on binary interactions and dynamics-based data, but real-world data often involve coarse-grained interaction states and multi-body interactions.
method: The method formulates an optimization model based on the minimum description length principle, uses MCMC sampling to generate candidate configurations, builds a Bayesian network guided by minimum-entropy, and applies an iterative update strategy.
result: Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed method.
conclusion: The proposed Bayesian network reconstruction method can effectively infer higher-order network structures from low-resolution interaction state data.

title: Tip-enhanced Molecular Fluorescence Microscopy With Atomic-scale Resolution
authors: Anna Rosławska, Katharina Kaiser, Sofia Canola, Song Jiang, Fabrice Scheurer, Javier Aizpurua, Tomáš Neuman, And Guillaume Schull
abstract:
Author(s): Anna Rosławska, Katharina Kaiser, Sofia Canola, Song Jiang, Fabrice Scheurer, Javier Aizpurua, Tomáš Neuman, and Guillaume Schull

Scanning probe techniques have transformed our ability to study materials at the atomic scale, providing atom-by-atom views of surfaces. Tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy combines scanning probes with optical fluorescence. Such optical techniques normally have spatial resolution limited by the wavelength of the light used. However, using the scanning tip itself as a nanoscale optical antenna confines the electromagnetic field to the tip apex, achieving superresolution down to the atomic scale. Fluorescence is a fundamental probe of materials that reveals electronic structure and vibronic properties by exciting electrons to higher levels and observing the photons emitted when they relax. These capabilities are of particular interest for studying and identifying molecules, submolecular structures, and their reactions. This review discusses the techniques of tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy and the new insights they have revealed.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 98, 025007] Published Tue Jun 30, 2026.
tldr: This review discusses tip-enhanced molecular fluorescence microscopy achieving atomic-scale resolution using scanning probe techniques.
motivation: To overcome the diffraction limit in optical microscopy and achieve atomic-scale resolution for studying molecular electronic and vibronic properties.
method: Combines scanning probe microscopy with a metallic tip that acts as a nanoscale optical antenna to confine the electromagnetic field at the tip apex.
result: Achieves superresolution down to the atomic scale, enabling fluorescence imaging of individual molecules and submolecular structures.
conclusion: Tip-enhanced fluorescence microscopy provides a powerful tool for nanoscale optical characterization of molecular systems.

title: Neutron Stars And The Dense Matter Equation Of State
authors: Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, And Anna L. Watts
abstract:
Author(s): Katerina Chatziioannou, H. Thankful Cromartie, Stefano Gandolfi, Ingo Tews, David Radice, Andrew W. Steiner, and Anna L. Watts

Neutron stars, the remnants of supernova explosions, are the densest objects in the Universe. A typical neutron star has a mass between one and two solar masses, and a radius of around 12 km. The density at the center of the star is higher than that in atomic nuclei. As a result, the properties of neutron stars provide important information about the behavior of ordinary matter under extreme compression. In recent years, new information about neutron stars has emerged from two sources. The first is the observation of the gravitational-wave signal from the final inspiral of a coalescing binary neutron star. The second is a careful measurement of the x-ray pulse profile of a spinning neutron star. This review discusses these measurements and summarizes how they constrain masses, radii, and central densities. The results are compared to predictions based on calculations of the nuclear equation of state at densities comparable to that in atomic nuclei, which are then extrapolated to higher density. The review ends with an outlook on future observational opportunities.


[Rev. Mod. Phys. 97, 045007] Published Wed Dec 24, 2025.
tldr: A review of neutron star observations and the dense matter equation of state.
motivation: To understand the behavior of matter at extreme densities found in neutron stars.
method: Review of gravitational-wave and X-ray observations, compared to nuclear equation of state calculations.
result: Constraints on neutron star masses, radii, and central densities are summarized.
conclusion: Future observations will further constrain the dense matter equation of state.

Its theoretical appeal has inspired decades of intensive model building and experimental searches. Recent results have placed stringent bounds on the supersymmetric parameter space, sharpening the focus on the remaining viable models. This review surveys the current status and outlook for supersymmetry in light of experimental constraints and recent theoretical developments, and presents projections for the discovery potential of the High-Luminosity Large Hadron Collider across multiple search channels and a variety of well-motivated scenarios.

There are many nuclear reactions that are of central importance for stellar burning and element formation. In typical stars, these reactions take place at very low energy, and many of them have very small rates, making it difficult to measure them directly in the laboratory. On the theoretical side, the low-energy regime is governed by quantum-mechanical phenomena like tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects. This review summarizes the state of the art in the theory of low-energy nuclear reactions in stars and describes new ideas for studying these reactions on Earth.

method: The paper reviews theoretical approaches including quantum tunneling, near-threshold resonances, and interference effects, and discusses experimental techniques for studying these reactions.
result: The review provides a comprehensive overview of current theoretical and experimental methods for low-energy nuclear astrophysics.
conclusion: Advances in theory and experiment are needed to better understand stellar nuclear reactions and element formation.

title: Characterizing The Low Energy Breakdown In Interpreting Photoionization Delays
authors: Brock Grafstrom And Alexandra S Landsman
abstract: Typical attosecond pump–probe experiments utilize a combination of extreme ultraviolet and IR laser pulses to extract precise timing information of electron dynamics. For sufficiently high photoelectron energies it is typically assumed that Wigner and Coulomb–laser-coupling (CLC) delays are separable, adding up to the experimentally measured photoionization delay. However, no widespread consensus has been reached on how to best interpret time delays at low photoelectron energies or IR wavelengths shorter than 800 nm. These questions are becoming crucial for the interpretation of state of the art ultrafast experiments in atoms and molecules studying electronic motion in bound and quasi-resonant states, where the dynamics of interest are typically only present within the low-energy portion of time delay spectra. In this work we provide an analytical cut-off law which describes the minimum energy where it is valid to approximate the total delay as the sum of the Wigner and CLC components for a given probe laser frequency. In doing so, we discover that the breakdown between the short-range (Wigner) and long-range (CLC) delay components begins around 23 eV for IR wavelengths near 400 nm. This energy is markedly higher than what is traditionally assumed, and therefore has important implications for interpretation of photoionization delay experiments probed with visible light.
tldr: This paper studies photoionization delays in attosecond pump-probe experiments, focusing on the breakdown of the separability of Wigner and Coulomb-laser-coupling delays at low photoelectron energies.
motivation: Interpreting time delays in ultrafast experiments is crucial for understanding electron dynamics, but no consensus exists for low energies or short IR wavelengths.
method: The authors derive an analytical cut-off law that defines the minimum energy where the total delay can be approximated as the sum of Wigner and CLC components for a given probe laser frequency.
result: The breakdown between short-range and long-range delay components begins around 23 eV for IR wavelengths near 400 nm, higher than traditionally assumed.
conclusion: The findings have important implications for interpreting photoionization delay experiments probed with visible light, especially in low-energy regimes.

authors: Adam R. Harris, Armin Kianfar, David Roca, Daniel Yago, Christoph Brehm, And Mahmoud I. Hussein
abstract:
Author(s): Adam R. Harris, Armin Kianfar, David Roca, Daniel Yago, Christoph Brehm, and Mahmoud I. Hussein

Super-resonance maintains a broadband out-of-phase response well beyond the characteristic bandwidth of conventional resonance, enabling broadband flow stabilization among other applications.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021045] Published Thu May 28, 2026.
tldr: This paper introduces a concept of super-resonance that breaks the bandwidth limit of resonant modes and applies it to flow control.
motivation: Conventional resonance has a limited bandwidth, which restricts its application in flow control and other areas. The authors aim to overcome this limitation.
method: The authors propose a super-resonance mechanism that maintains a broadband out-of-phase response beyond the characteristic bandwidth, and they demonstrate its application to flow stabilization.
result: Super-resonance enables broadband flow stabilization and other applications by breaking the traditional bandwidth limit of resonant modes.
conclusion: Super-resonance provides a new paradigm for resonant systems with potential applications in flow control and beyond.

A continuum theory that describes how mechanical metamaterials deform on surfaces takes the form of the Schrödinger equation and provides a different path for materials design.

title: Using Folded Proteins As Mechanically Well-Defined Units To Understand Fatigue Fracture In Hydrogels: Bridging Single Molecule And Bulk Studies
authors: Liang Dong, Puyu Cao, Huiyan Chen, Yu Zhang, Ying Li, Bin Chen, Yi Cao, And Hai Lei
abstract:
Author(s): Liang Dong, Puyu Cao, Huiyan Chen, Yu Zhang, Ying Li, Bin Chen, Yi Cao, and Hai Lei

A force-response model helps understand fatigue behavior and provides a design strategy for fatigue resistant hydrogels and soft materials.


[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021031] Published Mon May 11, 2026.
tldr: This paper studies fatigue fracture in hydrogels using folded proteins as mechanically well-defined units, bridging single-molecule and bulk experiments.
motivation: Understanding fatigue fracture in soft materials is crucial for designing durable hydrogels, but the molecular mechanisms are poorly understood.
method: The authors use folded proteins as model units to probe mechanical fatigue at the single-molecule level and relate it to bulk hydrogel behavior.
result: A force-response model is developed that explains fatigue behavior and provides design strategies for fatigue-resistant hydrogels.
conclusion: The work offers a molecular-level understanding of fatigue in hydrogels and a framework for designing tougher soft materials.

[Phys. Rev. X 16, 021024] Published Fri May 01, 2026.

motivation: To directly observe and characterize ion diffusion in superionic conductors at ultrafast timescales, linking microscopic dynamics to macroscopic properties.

motivation: Understanding how mechanical forces at topological defects drive cell extrusion in curved tissues is important for developmental biology and disease.

result: They find that curvature and topological defects create localized stresses that promote cell bulging and subsequent extrusion.
